Abstract

Modern multi-tenant cloud and enterprise operating systems suffer from severe latency degradation during workload surges due to the fundamentally reactive nature of standard CPU scheduling and resource-control frameworks. Existing mechanisms, such as the Linux Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) bandwidth control (cpu.max) and container quota controllers, adjust allocations only after run-queue contention, CPU throttling, or thread queueing has already occurred. This study develops and evaluates Adapt, an intelligent proactive resource-management framework that decouples predictive time-series machine learning into a user-space supervisory daemon while actuating standard Linux cgroups v2 resource bandwidth controllers ahead of workload demand.

We formulate a leak-free telemetry processing pipeline using chronological windowing and evaluate five standard time-series machine learning and deep learning algorithms—Support Vector Regression (SVR), Random Forest (RF), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Gated Recurrent Units (GRU)—alongside an ultra-fast statistical forecaster. Using empirical traces representing bursty enterprise cloud workloads, the proposed framework demonstrates substantial improvements over reactive baselines: 95th-percentile (P95) queuing latency is reduced from $15.54\text{ ms}$ (CFS-like reactive control) and $1,423.58\text{ ms}$ (reactive daemon) down to $9.94\text{ ms}$ ($36.0\%$ and $99.3\%$ reductions, respectively), SLA violations are completely eliminated ($0.0\%$ vs. $33.0\%$ under static quotas), and cumulative CPU throttled duration is reduced by $37.5\%$ to $87.2\%$.

Furthermore, we conduct an extensive component ablation study demonstrating that asymmetric hysteresis suppresses actuator thrashing by $11.3\times$ ($3$ vs. $34$ allocation events), while proactive headroom buffering prevents tail-latency doubling ($18.70\text{ ms}$ vs. $39.64\text{ ms}$). Explainable AI analysis using TreeSHAP establishes that I/O bandwidth accounts for $48.48\%$ of predictive importance, serving as a critical leading indicator for upcoming compute surges. The entire supervisory decision loop operates with an overhead below $0.15\text{ ms}$ per $1,000\text{ ms}$ epoch ($<0.015\%$ CPU consumption). The primary system limitation resides in user-to-kernel sysfs boundary write latencies and adaptation to unannounced distributional concept drift.

Keywords: Operating Systems Resource Management, Time-Series Forecasting, Project-Based Learning, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Proactive Scheduling, Explainable AI, Cgroups v2, CFS Bandwidth Control.

CHAPTER 1INTRODUCTION & PROBLEM FORMULATION

1.1 Context and Evolution of Operating System Scheduling

Operating systems serve as the critical interface between physical computing hardware and user-space execution threads. In multi-tenant environments—such as containerized Kubernetes clusters and cloud servers—the primary challenge is allocating CPU bandwidth fairly and predictably among competing workloads. To enforce multi-tenant isolation, modern Linux distributions employ Control Groups (cgroups), which regulate thread runtime via bandwidth controllers like the Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) bandwidth control.

1.2 The "Reactive Latency Tax" in Multi-Tenant Systems

Despite substantial advancements in kernel schedulers, resource control in existing commercial operating systems is fundamentally reactive. When an interactive service experiences an unexpected surge in incoming requests, the execution flow follows a cycle of delayed reaction:

Figure 1.1: The Reactive Latency Tax vs. Proactive Resource Provisioning. Reactive schedulers delay quota expansion until throttling has occurred, whereas Adapt anticipates bursts to maintain sub-10ms latency.

As illustrated in Figure 1.1, the sequence proceeds as follows:

  1. Demand Surge: Active threads rapidly consume their designated CFS bandwidth quota within the current $100\text{ ms}$ enforcement period.
  2. Kernel Throttling: Upon exhausting the quota, the Linux kernel removes the container's task group from the runnable tree, suspending execution until period replenishment.
  3. Queuing Latency Penalty: Incoming requests accumulate in kernel socket buffers, causing the 95th-percentile (P95) and 99th-percentile (P99) response latencies to spike dramatically, violating Service Level Agreements (SLAs).
  4. Delayed Reactive Allocation: Monitoring daemons or autoscalers detect the elevated CPU load only after a monitoring delay ($1\text{ to }15\text{ seconds}$) and subsequently scale the quota.

This persistent delay represents the Reactive Latency Tax, which degrades responsiveness in modern microservice architectures.

1.3 The In-Kernel Machine Learning Dilemma

While time-series forecasting could predict upcoming resource bursts, executing machine learning models directly inside the Linux kernel hot path is technically infeasible:

  • Floating-Point Restrictions: Core kernel interrupt handlers and scheduler routines strictly prohibit floating-point arithmetic without expensive register context-switching overheads.
  • Sub-Microsecond Latency Budgets: The scheduling dispatch loop (schedule()) executes in microsecond or sub-microsecond intervals. Evaluating complex neural networks or tree ensembles inside this loop would degrade system throughput.
  • Kernel Panic Risks: Machine learning libraries involve dynamic memory allocation and complex tensor operations. An unhandled mathematical fault, division by zero, or memory leak would trigger an immediate kernel panic.
Figure 1.2: Decoupled Two-Tier OS Architecture Block Diagram. Tier-1 user-space supervisory daemon handles forecasting and policy logic, actuating Tier-2 kernel cgroups via standard sysfs interfaces.

1.4 Research Objectives and Questions

To overcome this dilemma, we propose Adapt, a two-tier decoupled framework (Figure 1.2) that performs time-series forecasting and policy evaluation within a user-space supervisory daemon while actuating standard Linux cgroups v2 resource bandwidth controllers ahead of demand.

This thesis investigates five core research questions:

  • RQ1: Does proactive resource allocation driven by near-future demand forecasting significantly reduce OS tail latency and throttling compared with reactive baselines?
  • RQ2: Which time-series machine learning algorithm provides the optimal operational trade-off between predictive accuracy and inference execution latency?
  • RQ3: What is the quantitative contribution of asymmetric hysteresis in preventing actuator thrashing?
  • RQ4: How resilient is the proactive framework to sudden step contention and unannounced concept drift?
  • RQ5: What is the exact execution overhead across the user-to-kernel actuation boundary?

1.5 Measurable Contributions

  1. Decoupled Two-Tier Architecture: A verified separation between user-space supervisory intelligence and kernel-space cgroups enforcement.
  2. Empirical 5-Model Benchmark: Comparative evaluation of SVR, Random Forest, XGBoost, LSTM, and GRU under strict non-leaking chronological splits.
  3. Asymmetric Hysteresis Control: An anti-thrashing damping algorithm that enables rapid scale-up while enforcing a cooldown timer on scale-down.
  4. Deterministic Safety Guard & Drift Detection: CUSUM sequential drift detection with automated fallback to guaranteed safe reactive quotas.
  5. TreeSHAP Explainability: Proof that multi-metric telemetry provides superior predictive power, with I/O bandwidth identified as the dominant leading indicator ($48.48\%$ attribution) for future CPU demand.

CHAPTER 2LITERATURE REVIEW & THEORETICAL BACKGROUND

2.1 Evolution of Linux CPU Schedulers (O(1), CFS, EEVDF)

Operating system CPU scheduling has advanced through distinct paradigms over the past three decades:

Figure 2.1: Evolution of Operating System Scheduling Paradigms from early priority arrays to fair-queuing and decoupled intelligent control.

As illustrated in Figure 2.1, the progression includes:

  • The $O(1)$ Scheduler (Linux 2.6): Utilized dual active and expired priority bitmask arrays, achieving constant-time task selection at the cost of complex interactive heuristics.
  • The Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS, Linux 2.6.23 to 6.5): Introduced virtual runtime ($vruntime$) tracked via a red-black tree, maintaining proportional fair-share allocation across active tasks.
  • The EEVDF Scheduler (Linux 6.6+): Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First incorporates task eligibility and lag, ensuring bounded dispatch latency for interactive threads.
  • The Adapt Framework (This Research): Rather than modifying per-thread dispatch inside the kernel, Adapt operates at the resource-control tier, proactively adjusting aggregate cgroups bandwidth quotas ahead of incoming bursts.

2.2 Bandwidth Enforcement in Linux Cgroups v2

In Linux cgroups v2, CPU bandwidth allocation is controlled via the sysfs interface:

$$\text{/sys/fs/cgroup//cpu.max} = [\text{quota},\ \text{period}]$$

where $\text{period}$ defaults to $100,000\ \mu\text{s}$ ($100\text{ ms}$) and $\text{quota}$ dictates the maximum allowable CPU execution time across all cores. When a container's cumulative execution exceeds its quota, the kernel throttles the task group until the next period replenishment.

2.3 User-Space and Extensible Schedulers

Recent systems research has explored delegating scheduling policies outside the core kernel. Google's ghOSt [4] framework demonstrated that custom scheduling policies implemented in user space can guide thread execution via shared-memory message queues. Similarly, the BPF-sched_ext [25] subsystem (Linux 6.12+) enables dynamic loading of eBPF-based schedulers. Adapt builds on this architectural philosophy using standard, unmodified cgroups v2 interfaces.

2.4 Time-Series ML in Systems Engineering

Machine learning has been studied for cluster-level VM autoscaling (e.g., Microsoft's Resource Central [2]). However, cluster autoscaling operates on multi-minute timescales (VM spin-up times). In contrast, Adapt operates on sub-second to second timescales, optimizing local OS bandwidth quotas before kernel-level throttling degrades service quality.

CHAPTER 3SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE & DECOUPLED DESIGN

3.1 The Two-Tier Decoupled Architectural Principle

Adapt strictly separates predictive intelligence from low-level kernel execution. The supervisory control loop operates as follows:

Figure 3.2: Deterministic Safety Guard Finite State Machine (FSM). Dynamic confidence scoring and CUSUM drift detection trigger safe fallback mode automatically.

3.2 Policy Engine Formulation

The policy engine computes the target allocation $A(t)$ through three mathematical stages:

1. Proactive Headroom Buffering

Given the predicted demand $\hat{y}(t+k)$, the target proactive allocation incorporates a headroom buffer $\alpha = 0.15$ to absorb point-forecast uncertainty:

$$A_{\text{target}}(t) = \min\left(A_{\max},\ \max\left(A_{\min},\ \hat{y}(t+k) \cdot (1 + \alpha)\right)\right)$$

where $A_{\min} = 10.0\%$ (starvation floor) and $A_{\max} = 100.0\%$ (hardware ceiling).

2. Asymmetric Hysteresis Control

To eliminate actuator thrashing, allocation changes must exceed a minimum threshold $\Delta_{\min} = 8.0\%$, with scale-down constrained by a cooldown timer ($\text{cooldown\_ticks} = 3$ epochs):

$$A(t) = \begin{cases} A_{\text{target}}(t) & \text{if } A_{\text{target}}(t) > A_{\text{current}}(t) \text{ and } \Delta \ge \Delta_{\min} \\ A_{\text{target}}(t) & \text{if } A_{\text{target}}(t) < A_{\text{current}}(t),\ \Delta \ge \Delta_{\min},\ \text{and } \text{cooldown} \le 0 \\ A_{\text{current}}(t) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

3.3 Deterministic Safety Guard & CUSUM Concept Drift Detector

The safety subsystem continuously monitors prediction quality:

  • Confidence Estimator: Decays exponentially with normalized forecast error: $$C(t) = \exp\left(-\lambda \cdot \frac{|\hat{y}(t) - y(t)|}{\max(1.0, y(t))}\right)$$ If $C(t) < 0.40$, the Safety Guard triggers fallback mode.
  • CUSUM Drift Detector: Tracks cumulative error drift: $$S_t = \max\left(0, S_{t-1} + (e_t - \mu_{\text{train}}) - \kappa\right)$$ If $S_t > \tau_{\text{drift}} = 50.0$, concept drift is declared, and the system temporarily reverts to a reactive safety allocation ($y(t) \cdot 1.25$).

4.3 Zero-Leakage Chronological Sliding-Window Pipeline

To prevent lookahead data leakage:

  1. Chronological Partitioning: The dataset is split sequentially: Train ($70\%$), Validation ($15\%$), and Test ($15\%$). Shuffling is strictly prohibited.
  2. Train-Only Standardization: Normalization parameters ($\mu_{\text{train}}, \sigma_{\text{train}}$) are computed strictly on the training partition.
  3. Sliding-Window Sequences: With history window $W = 12$ and horizon $H = 3$, each feature tensor $X_i \in \mathbb{R}^{12 \times 5}$ maps to future demand $y_i = \text{cpu}(t_i + 3)$.

6.3 Queuing Latency, Throttling, and SLA Violations

As detailed in Table 6.2 and Figures 6.2 through 6.4:

  • Tail Latency Reduction: Adapt achieved a P95 latency of $9.94\text{ ms}$, representing a 36.0% reduction compared to CFS-like reactive control ($15.54\text{ ms}$) and a 99.3% reduction compared to the reactive daemon ($1423.58\text{ ms}$).
  • SLA Violation Elimination: Both CFS-like reactive control and Adapt maintained zero SLA violations ($0.0\%$), whereas static quota and reactive daemons breached the $45\text{ ms}$ threshold in $33\%$ and $41\%$ of epochs.
  • Throttling Mitigation: Adapt reduced cumulative throttled time to $5.0\text{ seconds}$, an improvement of 37.5% over CFS-like reactive control ($8.0\text{ s}$) and 87.2% over the reactive daemon ($39.0\text{ s}$).

7.2 Isolating Asymmetric Hysteresis

Disabling asymmetric hysteresis caused allocation adjustments to increase from 3 to 34 (an 11.3-fold increase in actuator thrashing). Frequent sysfs writes induce spinlock contention in kernel task groups. Hysteresis dampens these oscillations with negligible latency impact.

7.3 Isolating Proactive Headroom

Removing proactive headroom ($\alpha = 0.0$) caused throttled duration to jump from $6.0\text{ s}$ to **$20.0\text{ s}$ (a 3.3-fold surge)** and doubled P99 latency from $18.70\text{ ms}$ to **$39.64\text{ ms}$**. This confirms that the $15\%$ headroom factor is critical for absorbing forecast errors during burst ascents.

8.2 Systems Engineering Insights

  1. I/O as a Leading Indicator: Storage and network I/O accounted for nearly half ($48.48\%$) of the predictive weight. In cloud microservices, network packet reception and disk reads precede active CPU computation (data parsing and serialization), making I/O spikes a reliable early indicator of upcoming processor demand.
  2. The Value of Multivariate Telemetry: Traditional reactive OS schedulers monitor only current CPU utilization. TreeSHAP proves that over **$77\%$ of the predictive signal** originates from complementary dimensions (io_rate, memory_utilization, and request_rate), validating the multivariate telemetry architecture.

CHAPTER 9 & 10SOFTWARE PLATFORM, CONCLUSION & FUTURE WORK

9.1 Software Architecture and Automated Verification

The Adapt framework is structured into modular Python packages under adapt/. An automated test suite comprising 20 unit and integration tests (tests/test_adapt_suite.py) validates temporal non-leakage, tensor shapes, confidence degradation heuristics, and dry-run actuator safety in under 6 seconds.

10.1 Summary of Findings

This thesis presented the design, implementation, and empirical evaluation of Adapt, a proactive, forecast-driven resource-management framework for operating systems. By decoupling time-series forecasting into user space and actuating standard Linux cgroups v2 bandwidth limits ahead of demand, Adapt resolves the structural trade-off between reactive scheduling latency and kernel stability.

Key experimental findings include:

  • P95 latency reduction of 36.0% compared to CFS-like reactive resource control and 99.3% compared to reactive daemons.
  • Complete elimination of SLA violations ($0.0\%$ vs. $33.0\%$ under static quotas).
  • Throttling duration reduced by up to 87.2%.
  • Actuator thrashing suppressed by 11.3x through asymmetric hysteresis.
  • End-to-end control overhead below 0.15 ms, satisfying the sub-0.1% CPU budget for a 1-second control epoch.

10.2 Threats to Validity and Technical Limitations

  1. User-to-Kernel Boundary Overhead: Writing to /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max incurs a VFS file write ($0.045\text{ to }0.120\text{ ms}$). While negligible for 1-second epochs, sub-10-millisecond control cycles would require in-kernel communication.
  2. Polling Granularity: Telemetry is sampled at discrete 1-second intervals. Micro-bursts lasting under $10\text{ ms}$ cannot be captured by user-space polling and must still rely on kernel CFS fair queuing.
  3. Hardware Resource Contention: The current framework regulates CPU execution time quotas, but does not control shared L3 cache allocation (Intel RDT) or memory bus saturation.

10.3 Future Research Directions: eBPF BPF-sched_ext

Future work will focus on integrating Adapt with BPF-sched_ext (introduced in Linux 6.12). Rather than modifying quotas through sysfs, the user-space daemon could communicate through an eBPF ring buffer or shared memory array, allowing proactive policies to guide kernel run-queue dispatch directly with sub-microsecond latency.
